title: The Neck Swelling
case: A 24-year-old man from a rural area near a game park in Western Kenya presents with a two-month history of intermittent fever, headache, and general malaise. On examination, the following is noted at the neck.
fig: Posterior triangle neck swelling: Winterbottom's sign

qs.q: Identify the sign and give the single most likely diagnosis.
a: **Sign:** Winterbottom's sign, painless enlargement of the posterior cervical (posterior triangle) lymph nodes
**Diagnosis:** Human African Trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness), likely *T. b. rhodesiense* given East African distribution

qs.q: What is the vector, and what are the two clinical stages of this disease?
a: **Vector:** tsetse fly (*Glossina* species)
**Stage 1 (haemolymphatic):** fever, headache, Winterbottom's sign, trypanosomal chancre at the bite site
**Stage 2 (neurological/meningoencephalitic):** once the parasite crosses the blood-brain barrier: day/night sleep reversal, confusion, tremors, coma

qs.q: List the investigations you would order.
a: Thick and thin blood smear to identify trypomastigotes
Lymph node aspirate microscopy (enlarged posterior cervical node)
CSF analysis (lumbar puncture): mandatory to stage disease; look for cells, protein and trypanosomes
Card Agglutination Test for Trypanosomiasis (CATT): screening for *T. b. gambiense*
Full blood count: anaemia, thrombocytopenia

qs.q: Outline the treatment plan.
a: **Stage 1 (no CNS involvement):** pentamidine (*T.b. gambiense*) or suramin (*T.b. rhodesiense*)
**Stage 2 (CNS involvement):** melarsoprol, or nifurtimox-eflornithine combination therapy (NECT) for gambiense disease
Supportive care: antipyretics, seizure control if encephalopathy
Notify as a reportable communicable disease; vector control advice

title: The Breathless Patient
tag: Massive Left Pleural Effusion · CXR Interpretation
case: A 55-year-old man presents with a three-week history of progressive breathlessness, left-sided chest heaviness, and low-grade fever. His chest X-ray is shown below.
fig: Erect chest X-ray showing near-complete opacification of the left hemithorax

qs.q: Describe the film and give your diagnosis.
a: Dense homogeneous opacification of the left hemithorax with loss of the left costophrenic angle and hemidiaphragm outline
Mediastinal structures pushed towards the right (contralateral) side, indicating a large-volume effusion rather than collapse
**Diagnosis:** massive left-sided pleural effusion

qs.q: What physical examination findings would you expect over the left hemithorax?
a: **Inspection:** reduced chest wall movement, may be full/bulging
**Palpation:** trachea and apex beat deviated away from the effusion; reduced tactile fremitus
**Percussion:** stony dull note
**Auscultation:** reduced/absent breath sounds, reduced vocal resonance; bronchial breathing may be heard just above the fluid level

qs.q: List causes of a massive/unilateral pleural effusion.
a: **Exudative (protein-rich):**
Tuberculous pleural effusion (common cause in Kenya)
Parapneumonic effusion / empyema
Malignancy: bronchogenic carcinoma, mesothelioma, metastatic disease
**Transudative (usually bilateral, rarely massive):**
Congestive cardiac failure, nephrotic syndrome, liver cirrhosis, hypoalbuminaemia

qs.q: Outline your investigation and management plan.
a: **Diagnostic pleural tap:** Light's criteria to classify exudate vs transudate; cytology, AFB/GeneXpert, culture, ADA (raised in TB)
Therapeutic thoracocentesis if respiratory distress: drain slowly (<1.5 L at a time) to avoid re-expansion pulmonary oedema
Chest tube/intercostal drain if empyema or complicated parapneumonic effusion
Treat the underlying cause: anti-TB therapy, antibiotics, oncology referral as indicated
Pleurodesis for recurrent malignant effusions

title: The Distended Abdomen
case: A 48-year-old man with a background of chronic heavy alcohol use presents with progressive abdominal distension. On exposing the abdomen, the following is seen.
fig: Dilated periumbilical veins radiating from the umbilicus: caput medusae

qs.q: Name the sign and explain the mechanism behind it.
a: **Sign:** caput medusae, dilated tortuous superficial abdominal veins radiating from the umbilicus

**Mechanism:** portal hypertension causes recanalisation of the paraumbilical veins (of Sappey), shunting portal blood into the systemic circulation via the umbilical vein remnant, giving engorged periumbilical collaterals

qs.q: List the causes of ascites.
a: **High SAAG (≥1.1 g/dL), portal hypertension related:**
Cirrhosis (commonest cause overall)
Congestive cardiac failure / constrictive pericarditis
Budd-Chiari syndrome
Nephrotic syndrome (occasionally low SAAG)
**Low SAAG (<1.1 g/dL):**
Tuberculous peritonitis
Peritoneal carcinomatosis
Pancreatic ascites
Nephrotic syndrome / severe hypoalbuminaemia

qs.q: What investigations would you carry out for an ascitic patient?
a: **Diagnostic paracentesis:** cell count/differential (neutrophils ≥250/mm³ suggests SBP), albumin (for SAAG), total protein, Gram stain/culture, cytology, ADA
Abdominal ultrasound: confirm ascites, assess liver texture, portal vein patency, splenomegaly, masses
Liver function tests, albumin, clotting profile (INR)
Renal function tests and electrolytes
Viral hepatitis screen (HBsAg, anti-HCV)
Echocardiography if a cardiac cause is suspected

qs.q: Outline the management of ascites.
a: **Dietary:** sodium restriction (<2 g/day)
**Diuretics:** spironolactone ± furosemide (ratio 100:40), titrated to weight loss of about 0.5 kg/day (no peripheral oedema) or 1 kg/day (with oedema)
**Large-volume paracentesis** for tense/refractory ascites, with albumin replacement (about 6-8 g per litre removed beyond 5 L)
Treat the underlying cause (e.g. alcohol cessation, antivirals for viral hepatitis)
SBP prophylaxis in select patients (e.g. prior SBP, low ascitic protein): norfloxacin
TIPS or liver transplant referral for refractory cases

title: The Fingers and the Breathless Patient
tag: Finger Clubbing · Miliary TB · Central Cyanosis · Oxygen Therapy
case: A 30-year-old HIV-positive woman presents with chronic productive cough, weight loss, night sweats, and breathlessness. Her hands are shown below.
fig: Normal finger contour (left) vs clubbed finger with loss of Lovibond's angle (right)

qs.q: Describe the grades of finger clubbing.
a: **Grade 1:** fluctuation and softening of the nail bed
**Grade 2:** loss of the normal <165° angle between nail and nail bed (Lovibond's angle obliterated)
**Grade 3:** increased convexity of the nail fold, drumstick appearance
**Grade 4:** hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, thickening/swelling of the wrist/ankle with periosteal new bone formation

qs.q: This patient's chest X-ray shows a fine, diffuse micronodular (millet-seed) pattern. What is the diagnosis, and how would you confirm it?
a: **Diagnosis:** miliary tuberculosis, haematogenous dissemination of *M. tuberculosis*, common in immunosuppressed/HIV patients
Sputum GeneXpert MTB/RIF, AFB smear/culture
CXR: diffuse 1-3 mm nodules (millet seeds) throughout both lung fields
CT chest (more sensitive); tissue biopsy (liver/bone marrow) with histology showing caseating granulomas if the diagnosis is unclear
Fundoscopy for choroidal tubercles; consider CSF analysis for TB meningitis

qs.q: List causes of finger clubbing relevant to this presentation, and causes of central cyanosis.
a: **Causes of clubbing:**
Respiratory: bronchiectasis, lung abscess, empyema, fibrosing alveolitis, lung cancer (rarely TB itself)
Cardiac: cyanotic congenital heart disease, infective endocarditis
GI: IBD, cirrhosis
Others: idiopathic, familial
**Causes of central cyanosis:**
Severe pneumonia/miliary TB with hypoxaemia
Advanced COPD, severe asthma exacerbation
Pulmonary embolism, ARDS
Right-to-left cardiac shunts (e.g. tetralogy of Fallot, Eisenmenger syndrome)
High altitude, methaemoglobinaemia

qs.q: Name conditions in which an oxygen mask/oxygen therapy would be indicated.
a: Severe pneumonia/miliary TB with SpO₂ <94% (or 88-92% target in chronic CO₂ retainers)
Acute severe asthma / COPD exacerbation with hypoxaemia
Acute pulmonary oedema / heart failure
Pulmonary embolism with hypoxaemia
ARDS, sepsis with respiratory compromise
Post-operative/peri-arrest hypoxaemia, carbon monoxide poisoning (high-flow)
**Types of oxygen delivery device:**
Nasal cannula: 1-6 L/min, about 24-40% FiO₂, for mild hypoxaemia
Simple face mask: 5-10 L/min, about 40-60% FiO₂
Venturi mask: precise, fixed FiO₂ (24-60%), preferred in COPD to avoid CO₂ narcosis
Non-rebreather mask with reservoir: up to 90-95% FiO₂, for severe hypoxaemia

title: The Cola-Coloured Urine
case: A 9-year-old boy presents 2 weeks after a sore throat with periorbital puffiness, reduced urine output, and dark urine. His urine sample is shown, and his BP is 150/98 mmHg.
fig: Urine sample showing gross haematuria (tea/cola-coloured urine)

qs.q: What is the syndrome being described, and what is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
a: **Syndrome:** nephritic syndrome: haematuria, hypertension, oliguria, oedema, mild proteinuria
**Likely diagnosis:** post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (post-infectious GN), given the preceding pharyngitis and a latency of about 2 weeks

qs.q: List the key features and investigations for this nephritic case.
a: Urinalysis/microscopy: dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, sub-nephrotic range proteinuria
Renal function tests: raised urea/creatinine if renal impairment
Serum complement (C3 low, C4 normal in PSGN), ASOT titres, throat swab/culture
Renal ultrasound; renal biopsy if atypical course, progressive renal failure, or diagnosis unclear

qs.q: What are the acute (emergency) indications for dialysis? (mnemonic AEIOU)
a: **A**cidosis: severe metabolic acidosis refractory to medical therapy
**E**lectrolyte imbalance: refractory hyperkalaemia (K⁺ >6.5 or ECG changes)
**I**ngestion/intoxication: dialysable toxins (e.g. methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates, lithium)
**O**verload of fluid: refractory pulmonary oedema
**U**raemia: uraemic encephalopathy, pericarditis, or bleeding diathesis

qs.q: What metabolic screen would you request for a patient on chronic dialysis, and list complications of dialysis.
a: **Metabolic screen:**
Urea, creatinine, eGFR
Electrolytes: K⁺, Na⁺, HCO₃⁻, Ca²⁺, phosphate, magnesium
Parathyroid hormone (PTH): renal bone disease
Full blood count: renal anaemia; iron studies
Albumin: nutritional status
Lipid profile, glucose (if diabetic)
**Complications of haemodialysis:** hypotension during session; vascular access infection/thrombosis (AV fistula); disequilibrium syndrome; anaemia, bone disease (long term); air embolism (rare)

**Complications of peritoneal dialysis:** peritonitis; catheter-site infection; protein loss / hypoalbuminaemia; membrane failure (ultrafiltration failure) over time; hernias from raised intra-abdominal pressure

note: Candidates should distinguish nephritic (haematuria, hypertension, oliguria) from nephrotic (heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, hyperlipidaemia) presentations. This is a very common OSCE trap.

title: The Swollen Ankles
case: A 60-year-old woman presents with bilateral ankle swelling that worsens through the day. On examination, sustained pressure over the pretibial region leaves a persistent indentation, shown below.
fig: Pretibial pitting oedema: indentation persists after finger pressure is released

qs.q: Define pitting oedema and describe how you would grade it.
a: **Definition:** accumulation of fluid in the interstitial space such that firm digital pressure for about 5 seconds leaves a visible indentation
**1+:** pit about 2 mm, recovers immediately
**2+:** pit about 4 mm, recovers in 10-15 seconds
**3+:** pit about 6 mm, recovers in 1-2 minutes
**4+:** pit about 8 mm, recovers in 2-5 minutes

qs.q: List the causes of bilateral pitting oedema.
a: **Cardiac:** congestive cardiac failure, constrictive pericarditis
**Renal:** nephrotic syndrome, chronic kidney disease with fluid overload
**Hepatic:** cirrhosis with hypoalbuminaemia
**Nutritional:** kwashiorkor / severe protein malnutrition
**Venous:** chronic venous insufficiency (usually unilateral or asymmetric)
**Drugs:** calcium channel blockers (amlodipine), NSAIDs, corticosteroids
**Endocrine/other:** hypothyroidism (usually non-pitting myxoedema), pregnancy-related (pre-eclampsia)

qs.q: Outline your bedside and laboratory workup.
a: Full clinical exam: JVP, heart sounds/murmurs, chest for effusions/crackles, hepatomegaly/ascites
Urinalysis: proteinuria (dipstick, urine protein:creatinine ratio)
Renal function tests, electrolytes, albumin
Liver function tests
Thyroid function tests
Echocardiography if a cardiac cause is suspected
Doppler ultrasound of the legs if a venous cause / DVT is suspected

qs.q: Briefly outline management principles.
a: Treat the underlying cause (heart failure therapy, manage nephrotic syndrome, correct hypoalbuminaemia)
Diuretics (loop ± thiazide) titrated to clinical response
Leg elevation, compression stockings for venous causes
Sodium and fluid restriction where fluid overload is the driver
Review and stop/adjust culprit medications where relevant

title: The Confused Patient with a Headache
case: A 34-year-old HIV-positive man with poor ART adherence presents with a two-week history of headache, low-grade fever, and new-onset right-sided weakness. A contrast CT brain is performed.
fig: Contrast CT brain showing a well-defined ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema and mass effect

qs.q: Describe the scan and give a differential diagnosis for a ring-enhancing brain lesion.
a: **Description:** rounded lesion with a hypodense centre, a thin enhancing rim, surrounding vasogenic oedema, and mass effect with midline shift
**Differential:**
Toxoplasmosis: most likely in this HIV patient (classically multiple lesions, basal ganglia)
Pyogenic brain abscess
Tuberculoma
Primary CNS lymphoma (often single lesion, periventricular)
Metastasis (usually multiple, at the grey-white junction)
Glioblastoma / high-grade glioma
Resolving haematoma, neurocysticercosis (in the right epidemiological context)

qs.q: What investigations would help narrow the diagnosis?
a: HIV test/CD4 count (if not already known)
Toxoplasma IgG serology
MRI brain with contrast: better characterisation than CT
Empirical anti-toxoplasma trial with repeat imaging at 2 weeks if HIV-positive with typical lesion(s); clinical/radiological improvement supports the diagnosis
CSF analysis (if safe, with no significant mass effect): cytology, AFB/GeneXpert, culture, cryptococcal antigen
Stereotactic brain biopsy if no response to empirical therapy or atypical features
Chest X-ray / CT to look for a primary malignancy or TB focus

qs.q: Outline your management plan.
a: **Empirical treatment for toxoplasmosis:** pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid (or co-trimoxazole where those are unavailable) for 6 weeks, then secondary prophylaxis until CD4 >200 for at least 6 months on ART
Dexamethasone for significant oedema/mass effect (short course, taper once improving)
Anticonvulsants if seizures
Initiate/optimise ART once the acute opportunistic infection is being treated (timing individualised to avoid IRIS)
If tuberculoma is suspected/confirmed: standard anti-TB therapy (extended duration for CNS TB) + steroids
Neurosurgical referral if an abscess needs drainage, or the lesion causes critical mass effect

note: In an HIV-positive patient with multiple ring-enhancing lesions, toxoplasmosis is treated empirically first-line; biopsy is reserved for those who fail to improve, as it carries higher risk and cost.
